notes.front: What is Git Large File Storage (LFS)?
notes.back: A tool that keeps pointers to large files in the repository and stores their binary content in separate remote storage.
notes.explanation: It downloads the right version when you clone or switch branches, so the team keeps its normal Git workflow.
notes.example: A game studio keeps its 200-megabyte texture files in Git LFS while its code stays in plain Git.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “What is Git Large File Storage (Git LFS)?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Git LFS: - Stores pointers to large files in your repo instead of the full file contents. - Stores the binary content in separate remote storage. - Downloads the correct version when you clone or switch branches. - Keeps your normal Git workflow for large binaries

notes.front: What is a Git LFS pointer file?
notes.back: The small file kept in the repository in place of a large file, acting as a reference to the real file stored elsewhere.
notes.explanation: When you clone, GitHub uses the pointer file as a map to find the large file for you.
notes.example: A three-line text file in the repository standing in for an 80-megabyte training video.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git Large File Storage”, “About Git Large File Storage”
notes.evidence: creates a pointer file which acts as a reference to the actual file (which is stored somewhere else). {% data variables.product.github %} manages this pointer file in your repository. When you clone the repository down, {% data variables.product.github %} uses the pointer file as a map to go and find the large file for you.

notes.front: What is git-fat?
notes.back: A tool that lets large binaries use the normal Git workflow while it manages those “fat” files separately from versioned files.
notes.explanation: Clones stay small and fast because no binaries are transferred, yet they keep complete metadata.
notes.example: Marking `*.psd` design files as fat, so designers commit them as usual while their content goes to a shared store.
notes.source: Jed Brown, “git-fat README”, “Features of git-fat” (jedbrown/git-fat on GitHub)
notes.evidence: clones of the source repository are small and fast because no binaries are transferred, yet fully functional with complete metadata and incremental retrieval (`git clone --depth` has limited granularity and couples metadata to content) * git-fat supports the same workflow for large binaries and traditionally versioned files, but internally manages the "fat" files separately

notes.front: What is Scalar?
notes.back: A Git tool for very large repositories that tunes advanced Git settings, runs maintenance in the background and cuts data sent over the network.
notes.explanation: You drive it with the `scalar` command and subcommands such as `clone`, `register` and `diagnose`.
notes.example: A developer on a monorepo with millions of files clones it through Scalar so everyday fetches stay quick.
notes.source: Git project, “scalar documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Scalar enlistment?
notes.back: The top-level directory of a Scalar project, which usually holds the Git working tree in a `src` subdirectory.
notes.explanation: Tracked files live inside `src`, apart from untracked files such as build output kept beside it.
notes.example: `~/work/bigrepo` is the enlistment, and `~/work/bigrepo/src` is the working tree.
notes.source: Git project, “scalar documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is git-sizer?
notes.back: A command-line tool that gives a high-level assessment of a repository’s size and complexity.
notes.explanation: It calculates repository-wide metrics and assigns a level of concern to each one.
notes.example: Running it before a migration to see which of the repository’s metrics are flagged as worrying.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “git-sizer” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use git-sizer for a high-level assessment of repository size and complexity. It calculates repository-wide metrics and assigns a level of concern to each one.

notes.front: What is a repository resource in an Azure Pipelines definition?
notes.back: An entry under `resources: repositories:` that declares another repository and gives it a name that `checkout` steps can use.
notes.explanation: Each entry sets the repository’s `type`, its `name` and, where needed, a service connection as its `endpoint`.
notes.example: Declaring a GitHub repository of shared scripts as `tools`, then adding the step `- checkout: tools`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Check out multiple repositories in your pipeline”, “Repository resource definition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - repository: MyGitHubRepo # The name used to reference this repository in the checkout step type: github endpoint: MyGitHubServiceConnection name: MyGitHubOrgOrUser/MyGitHubRepo

notes.front: What is a Git tag, and which two kinds does Azure DevOps support?
notes.back: A named marker for a specific commit; lightweight tags are just a pointer, annotated tags add tagger, message and date.
notes.explanation: Annotated tags record who tagged, when and why; the web portal creates only these, so lightweight tags come from the Git command line.
notes.example: `v2.4.0` marking the exact commit that shipped to customers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Git tags” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps supports both annotated and lightweight tags. Lightweight tags are a pointer to specific commit, while annotated tags contain more information such as the tagger, message, and date. You can create annotated tags using the web portal. You can create both lightweight and annotated tags from within Visual Studio.

notes.front: What does `git reflog` work with?
notes.back: Reference logs: records, kept in your local repository, of when branch tips and other references were updated.
notes.explanation: Other Git commands can use these entries to name an earlier value of a reference.
notes.example: Like a browser’s history for your branch pointers, kept only on your own machine.
notes.source: Git project, “git-reflog documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is `git filter-repo`?
notes.back: A history-rewriting tool that GitHub recommends for removing a file from a repository’s history.
notes.explanation: A file added in an earlier commit has to be taken out of the history, not just deleted in a new commit.
notes.example: Purging a database dump committed by mistake months ago from every commit before the repository is shared.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About large files on GitHub”, “Removing a file that was added in an earlier commit”
notes.evidence: If you added a file in an earlier commit, you need to remove it from the repository's history. To remove files from the repository's history, we recommend the git filter-repo command.

notes.front: According to the Azure Repos guidance, where should dependencies and reusable packages go instead of Git?
notes.back: Azure Artifacts package management.
notes.explanation: Source files, scripts and text files stay in Git, and large binaries that change often and don’t diff well go to Git LFS.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Decide where to store each file” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - Keep source files, scripts, and text files in Git. - Move dependencies and reusable packages to Azure Artifacts package management. - Use Git LFS for large binary files that change often and don't diff well.

notes.front: What are two kinds of output the Azure Repos guidance says not to commit to Git?
notes.back: Any two of: binaries, logs, tracing output, diagnostic data.
notes.explanation: Logs and trace information are shared through work item tracking or team file sharing instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Don’t commit build outputs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - Don't commit binaries, logs, tracing output, or diagnostic data. - Share logs and trace information through work item tracking or team file sharing.

notes.front: What does Azure DevOps Services charge for Git LFS?
notes.back: Nothing: it fully supports Git LFS and offers it for free.
notes.explanation: To use it you install the Git LFS client, configure tracking for the files, and push to Azure Repos.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Git LFS benefits” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps Services fully supports Git LFS and offers it for free. To use LFS, install the Git LFS client, configure tracking for the files you want to store in LFS, and then push your changes to Azure Repos.

notes.front: What three things does a Git LFS pointer file record?
notes.back: The Git LFS `version`, a unique identifier for the file (`oid`), and the file’s `size`.
notes.explanation: Those few lines are all that the repository holds for the large file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git Large File Storage”, “Pointer file format”
notes.evidence: It tracks the version of {% data variables.large_files.product_name_short %} you're using, followed by a unique identifier for the file (`oid`). It also stores the size of the final file.

notes.front: What does a clone get if the Git LFS client isn’t installed or configured correctly?
notes.back: Pointer data instead of the binary files.
notes.explanation: Every Git client must install the Git LFS client and understand its tracking configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Git LFS limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - Every Git client must install the Git LFS client and understand its tracking configuration. - If the client isn't installed or configured correctly, clones download pointer data instead of the binary file.

notes.front: In an Azure Repos repository that uses Git LFS, what happens if you drag a binary file into the web interface?
notes.back: The binary itself is committed to the repository, not the LFS pointer.
notes.explanation: A web upload therefore undoes the point of tracking that file with Git LFS.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Git LFS limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Dragging a binary file into the web interface commits the binary to the repo, not the LFS pointer.

notes.front: What happens when you push a file to GitHub that is above the warning size but below the block limit?
notes.back: Git warns you, but the changes still push successfully.
notes.explanation: GitHub suggests you consider removing the commit to minimise the effect on performance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About large files on GitHub”, “File size limits”
notes.evidence: you will receive a warning from Git. The changes will still successfully push to your repository, but you can consider removing the commit to minimize performance impact.

notes.front: GitHub warns about files larger than 50 MiB and blocks files larger than {{c1::100 MiB}}.
notes.explanation: These are the values the About large files on GitHub page inserts for its warning and block limits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “data variables “large_files.yml”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: warning_size: '50 MiB' max_github_size: '100 MiB'

notes.front: GitHub recommends that repositories stay small, ideally under {{c1::1 gigabyte}}, and strongly recommends under 5.
notes.explanation: Smaller repositories are faster to clone and easier to work with and maintain.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About large files on GitHub”, “Repository size limits”
notes.evidence: We recommend repositories remain small, ideally less than 1 GB, and less than 5 GB is strongly recommended. Smaller repositories are faster to clone and easier to work with and maintain.

notes.front: What does git-fat depend on?
notes.back: Only stock Python and rsync.
notes.explanation: Fat object stores can be shared between clones, and can be spread across several hosts.
notes.source: Jed Brown, “git-fat README”, “Features of git-fat” (jedbrown/git-fat on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * local fat object stores can be shared between multiple clones, even by different users * can easily support fat object stores distributed across multiple hosts * depends only on stock Python and rsync

notes.front: How do you tell git-fat which files are fat?
notes.back: List their extensions in `.gitattributes` with the `fat` filter, for example `*.png filter=fat -crlf`.
notes.explanation: The attributes file maps file patterns to the fat filter.
notes.source: Jed Brown, “git-fat README”, “Installation and configuration” (jedbrown/git-fat on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Edit (or create) .gitattributes to regard any desired extensions as fat files.

notes.front: Which commands synchronise git-fat’s fat files with the remote store?
notes.back: `git fat push` and `git fat pull`.
notes.explanation: Everything else uses normal Git commands, without thinking about which files are fat.
notes.source: Jed Brown, “git-fat README”, “Summary” (jedbrown/git-fat on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use normal git commands to interact with the repository without thinking about what files are fat and non-fat. The fat files will be treated specially. * Synchronize fat files with `git fat push` and `git fat pull`.

notes.front: Which objects does `scalar clone` download by default?
notes.back: Only commit and tree objects.
notes.explanation: Leaving file contents out of the initial clone is one of the ways Scalar reduces data sent over the network.
notes.source: Git project, “scalar documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After `scalar clone`, which files are in the working tree at first?
notes.back: Only the files in the top-level directory, because sparse-checkout is switched on.
notes.explanation: You widen it with `git sparse-checkout set`, or `git sparse-checkout disable` for every file.
notes.source: Git project, “scalar documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which `scalar clone` option stops sparse-checkout being set up?
notes.back: `--full-clone`.
notes.explanation: Without it, `scalar clone` always starts with a sparse working tree.
notes.source: Git project, “scalar documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why do large, frequently updated files hurt Git performance?
notes.back: Each change rewrites much of the file, so delta compression stops working and Git stores nearly a full snapshot each time.
notes.explanation: As a result, repository size and object count grow quickly.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Large and frequently updated files” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Because each change usually rewrites a large portion of the file, delta compression becomes ineffective and causes Git to store nearly a full snapshot for each revision. As a result, repository size and object count grow quickly.

notes.front: How many direct entries in a single directory does the guidance treat as a sign the structure needs rebalancing?
notes.back: More than a few hundred.
notes.explanation: The guidance asks you to keep the number of direct entries in any single directory manageable.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Oversized or flat directory structures” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Keep the number of direct entries in any single directory manageable. A count above a few hundred is a sign that the structure should be rebalanced.

notes.front: Why do many unused, long-lived branches slow down clones?
notes.back: `git clone` downloads objects reachable from every remote branch, including files never merged into `main`.
notes.explanation: Files that were never merged still travel with every clone.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Unused branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you `git clone` a repository, Git downloads objects reachable from every remote branch, including files that were never merged into `main`.

notes.front: Does deleting a branch or force pushing reclaim space in an Azure Repos repository?
notes.back: No. Storage is append-only; the only complete fix is to recreate the repository and migrate just the content you need.
notes.explanation: The performance advice prevents rapid future growth but doesn’t shrink a repository that has already grown.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Unused branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Repos storage is append-only on the server. The recommendations in this article prevent rapid future growth, but they don't shrink a repository that has already grown. Previously committed files and directories remain on the server. Force-pushing or deleting a branch doesn't reclaim that space.

notes.front: With default paths, what happens to the first repository’s location when you add a second `checkout` step?
notes.back: It moves from `s` into `s/<repository name>`.
notes.explanation: Scripts that relied on the old default path then need updating.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Check out multiple repositories in your pipeline”, “Checkout path” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you are using default paths, adding a second repository checkout step changes the default path of the code for the first repository.

notes.front: Which repositories can be named inline in a `checkout` step, such as `git://MyProject/MyRepo`?
notes.back: Only Azure Repos Git repositories in the same organisation.
notes.explanation: Other types, and Azure Repos in another organisation, need a service connection and a repository resource.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Check out multiple repositories in your pipeline”, “Inline syntax checkout” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Only Azure Repos Git repositories in the same organization can use the inline syntax. Azure Repos Git repositories in a different organization, and other supported repository types require a service connection and must be declared as a repository resource.

notes.front: Can a pipeline run scripts that live in the template repository?
notes.back: No: only the template files are used, and the expanded pipeline runs as if it were defined in the source repository.
notes.explanation: The same resource is used for the whole pipeline run.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use YAML templates in pipelines for reusable and secure processes”, “Store templates in other repositories” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After that, the same resource is used during the pipeline run. Only the template files are used. Once the templates are fully expanded, the final pipeline runs as if it were defined entirely in the source repo. This means that you can't use scripts from the template repo in your pipeline.

notes.front: If a template repository resource sets no `ref`, the pipeline uses {{c1::`refs/heads/main`}}.
notes.explanation: Following `main` means template changes reach your pipeline as soon as they merge.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use YAML templates in pipelines for reusable and secure processes”, “Store templates in other repositories” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If no `ref` is specified, the pipeline defaults to using `refs/heads/main`.

notes.front: What does the Not set permission state do in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: It neither grants nor denies; permissions from another group or a parent scope can still apply.
notes.explanation: It is the neutral choice: it leaves the decision to other assignments.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Understand permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Not set doesn't grant or deny the permission. Permissions assigned through another group or inherited from a parent scope can still apply.

notes.front: When does an Allow permission state fail to grant access?
notes.back: When a more specific or applicable Deny overrides it.
notes.explanation: Allow is therefore not the final word when a Deny applies.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Understand permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Allow grants the permission unless a more specific or applicable Deny overrides it.

notes.front: How does a Deny permission state behave?
notes.back: It generally overrides Allow, including inherited or group-granted Allow, and applies to every member of a denied group.
notes.explanation: One Deny on a group therefore reaches everyone in it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Understand permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Deny** generally overrides **Allow**, including permissions inherited or granted through another group. When you deny a permission for a group, the denial affects all members of that group.

notes.front: What happens when you turn off inheritance for a single Git repository?
notes.back: Permissions from the project-level Git repositories entry no longer flow to it.
notes.explanation: You should record the current setting first and check that the remaining assignments give the intended access.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Configure inheritance for a repository” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Before you change inheritance, record the current setting and review the repository's explicit and inherited permissions. When you turn off inheritance, permissions from the project-level Git repositories entry no longer flow to the repository.

notes.front: Which older permission did the two bypass permissions replace, and what was wrong with it?
notes.back: Exempt from policy enforcement; it also let users push directly to the branch and skip the pull request process entirely.
notes.explanation: It covered both completing pull requests and pushing, which the two new permissions separate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Configure policy bypass permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Previously, the Exempt from policy enforcement permission helped teams manage which users were granted the ability to bypass branch policies when they completed a pull request. However, that permission also granted users the ability to push directly to the branch and bypass the PR process entirely.

notes.front: Which kind of tag can you create in the Azure DevOps web portal?
notes.back: Only annotated tags; for a lightweight tag, the docs point to the Git command line.
notes.explanation: The portal’s Create tag form therefore asks for a description.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Git tags”, “Create tag” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can only create annotated tags in the web portal or Visual Studio. To create a lightweight tag, you can use Git command line.

notes.front: Why be careful about deleting a tag from the remote repository?
notes.back: Anyone who has pulled, forked or cloned the repository keeps the tag in their copy.
notes.explanation: The docs advise deleting only local tags, or ones you’re sure nobody has pulled, cloned or forked.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Git tags”, “Delete tag” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use caution when deleting tags from your repo. If the repo has been pulled, forked, or cloned by another user, the tag will still exist in their copy of the repo. You should only delete local tags, or if you are sure that the repo hasn't been pulled, cloned, or forked since you created your tag.

notes.front: When you create a tag from the Tags view in the web portal, which field is required because the tag is annotated?
notes.back: Description.
notes.explanation: You also give a name and choose the branch to tag from.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Git tags”, “Create tag” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Specify a **Name**, select the branch to **Tag from**, enter a **Description** (required since you're creating an annotated tag), and select **Create**.

notes.front: How do you create a branch from a tag in the Azure DevOps web portal?
notes.back: Select the … next to the tag and choose New branch.
notes.explanation: The new branch starts from the tagged commit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Git tags”, “Create branch from a tag” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To create a branch from a tag, select the ellipsis to the right of the tag name and choose **New branch**.

notes.front: What does `git reset --hard <commit>` do to later changes?
notes.back: Resets the branch to that commit and discards all later changes.
notes.explanation: The docs warn to be careful, since you can lose work with it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Revert a branch to a prior state” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The --hard flag tells Git to reset the branch to the specified commit, and to discard all subsequent changes. Be careful with this option since you can lose work using it.

notes.front: Which `git reset` flag is the default, and what does it keep?
notes.back: `--mixed`; it keeps all later changes as unstaged changes.
notes.explanation: The branch still moves back to the chosen commit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Revert a branch to a prior state” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The --mixed flag tells Git to reset the branch to the specified commit, but to keep all subsequent changes as unstaged changes. This option is the default.

notes.front: Which `git reset` flag keeps later changes staged and unstaged just as they were?
notes.back: `--soft`.
notes.explanation: Nothing is lost; only the branch pointer moves back.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Revert a branch to a prior state” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The --soft flag tells Git to reset the branch to the specified commit, but to keep all subsequent changes as staged and unstaged changes per their previous state.

notes.front: What does `git revert <commit>` do?
notes.back: Creates a new commit that reverses that commit’s changes; the original commit stays in history.
notes.explanation: Because history isn’t altered, local and remote branch histories continue to match.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Undo the changes made by a shared commit” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Git revert doesn't delete the original commit. This approach is suitable for undoing the changes made by a shared commit because Git revert won't alter the previous commit history, and so local and remote branch histories continue to match.

notes.front: In reflog notation, what does `HEAD@{2}` mean?
notes.back: Where `HEAD` was two moves ago.
notes.explanation: Similarly, `main@{one.week.ago}` means where `main` pointed a week ago in this local repository.
notes.source: Git project, “git-reflog documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How long after deletion can you restore a deleted Azure Repos branch?
notes.back: At any time: there’s no retention policy on deleted branches.
notes.explanation: Deleted branches can be found and restored from the Branches view whenever needed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Restore a deleted Git branch from the web portal”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: There's no retention policy on deleted branches. You can restore a deleted Git branch at any time, regardless of when it was deleted.

notes.front: Why doesn’t deleting a large file locally and committing again make the repository smaller for others?
notes.back: The file still exists in the repository’s history, so every clone still downloads it.
notes.explanation: Only rewriting the history removes it from what clones download.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remove a large binary from your Git history to manage the size of cloned repositories”, “Problem scenario” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Even if you remove the large file from your local repo and recommit, the file still exists in the repo's history. As a result, the file is still downloaded to everyone's local computer as part of the history.

notes.front: What is the first step before removing a large file from a shared repository’s history?
notes.back: Freeze the repo: ask the team to stop pushing to it.
notes.explanation: Any pushes made during the process must be accounted for, so no data is lost.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remove a large binary from your Git history to manage the size of cloned repositories”, “Freeze the repo” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Ask the team to stop pushing to the repo. If more pushes happen during this process, you must account for them so that you don't lose any data.

notes.front: Which `git-filter-repo` flag, and which minimum version, does GitHub’s sensitive-data procedure need?
notes.back: `--sensitive-data-removal`, in version 2.47 or later.
notes.explanation: You can install the tool manually or through a package manager.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Purging a file from your local repository's history using git-filter-repo”
notes.evidence: You need a version with the --sensitive-data-removal flag, meaning at least version 2.47. You can install git-filter-repo manually or by using a package manager.

notes.front: Which `git-filter-repo` options delete one file from every branch, tag and ref?
notes.back: `--sensitive-data-removal --invert-paths --path` followed by the file’s path in the repository.
notes.explanation: Use the file’s path in the repository, not just its file name.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Purging a file from your local repository's history using git-filter-repo”
notes.evidence: with the **git path to the file you want to remove, not just its filename** (e.g. `src/module/phone-numbers.txt`): ```shell git-filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --invert-paths --path PATH-TO-YOUR-FILE-WITH-SENSITIVE-DATA

notes.front: How can sensitive data return after you rewrite history and push?
notes.back: A colleague with an older clone runs `git pull` then `git push`, bringing the data back.
notes.explanation: They must discard and re-clone, or carefully clean up their clone first.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Side effects of rewriting history”
notes.evidence: If a fellow developer has a clone from before your rewrite, and after your rewrite simply runs `git pull` followed by `git push`, the sensitive data will return.  They need to either discard their clone and re-clone, or carefully walk through multiple steps to clean up their clone first.

notes.front: Which commits get new hashes when you rewrite history to remove sensitive data?
notes.back: The commits that introduced the data and all commits that came after.
notes.explanation: Any tooling or automation that relies on commit hashes staying the same can break.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Side effects of rewriting history”
notes.evidence: Rewriting history will change the hashes of the commits that introduced the sensitive data and all commits that came after. Any tooling or automation that depends on commit hashes not changing will be broken or have problems.

notes.front: What must happen to branch protections that block force pushes before you can remove sensitive data?
notes.back: They must be turned off, at least temporarily.
notes.explanation: The rewritten history can only reach GitHub through a force push.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Side effects of rewriting history”
notes.evidence: If you have any branch protections that prevent force pushes, those protections will have to be turned off (at least temporarily) for the sensitive data to be removed.

notes.front: A repository holds source code, a shared library other teams consume, and 300-megabyte video files edited every week. Where should the video files go?
notes.choices:
A) Plain Git
B) Azure Artifacts package management
C) A compressed archive committed to Git
D) Git LFS
notes.back: D) Git LFS
notes.choicesExplained: A stores a full copy of each video version and slows every clone. B is for dependencies and reusable packages, like the shared library. C is an archive, which the guidance says not to commit.
notes.explanation: Large binary files that change often are the case Git LFS is meant for.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Choose the right storage option for Git, package management, and Git LFS” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Large binary files that change often | Git LFS |

notes.front: A developer wants to commit the `bin/` build output and test logs so testers can grab them. What does the Azure Repos guidance say?
notes.choices:
A) Commit them to a separate branch
B) Don’t commit them; keep Git for source and share logs through work items or file sharing
C) Commit them through Git LFS
D) Commit them, then squash merge
notes.back: B) Don’t commit them; keep Git for source and share logs through work items or file sharing
notes.choicesExplained: A and D still put build output into the repository. C only changes where the content is stored; the guidance says build output doesn’t belong in the repo.
notes.explanation: Git is for source, not build output or test artefacts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Don’t commit build outputs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use Git for source, not build output or test artifacts. - Don't commit binaries, logs, tracing output, or diagnostic data. - Share logs and trace information through work item tracking or team file sharing.

notes.front: A team’s design sources are large files that change often and differ a lot between versions. They want to keep their Git workflow. What should they use?
notes.choices:
A) Squash merges
B) Shallow clones
C) A partial clone
D) Git LFS
notes.back: D) Git LFS
notes.choicesExplained: B and C reduce what one client downloads but still store every version in the repository. A reduces commits, not file sizes.
notes.explanation: Its pointers keep the repository small while the content lives in separate storage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “What is Git Large File Storage (Git LFS)?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use Git Large File Storage (LFS) for source files that change often and differ significantly between versions.

notes.front: After cloning, a colleague opens a large asset and finds three lines starting `version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1`. What is the likely cause?
notes.choices:
A) The file was corrupted during the push
B) The repository uses git-fat
C) The version line points to a missing download
D) The Git LFS client isn’t installed or configured on her machine
notes.back: D) The Git LFS client isn’t installed or configured on her machine
notes.choicesExplained: A the three lines are a valid pointer file, not corruption. C the version value only defines the pointer file type; it isn’t a link. B git-fat placeholders look different.
notes.explanation: Without a working client, clones download pointer data instead of the binary.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Git LFS file format” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The GitHub URL included for the version value only defines the LFS pointer file type. It's not a link to your binary file.

notes.front: Two artists edited the same Git LFS-tracked texture on separate branches, and now the merge fails. What does the Azure Repos guidance say about this?
notes.choices:
A) Git LFS merges binary files automatically
B) Switching to Secure Shell fixes it
C) Git can’t merge different versions of a binary, so teammates must coordinate changes
D) A squash merge will combine the two versions
notes.back: C) Git can’t merge different versions of a binary, so teammates must coordinate changes
notes.choicesExplained: A is false: Git can’t merge binary versions. B isn’t supported for Git LFS in Azure Repos. D can’t merge binary content either.
notes.explanation: File locking helps, but users still need to pull the latest copy before they begin.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Git LFS limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - Git can't merge different versions of a binary file, so teammates still need to coordinate changes. - Git LFS provides file locking, but users still need to pull the latest copy before they begin work.

notes.front: A developer can clone most Azure Repos repositories over Secure Shell, but one that tracks files with Git LFS won’t work that way. Why?
notes.choices:
A) Her Secure Shell key has expired
B) The repository has too many branches
C) Git LFS needs a partial clone
D) Azure Repos doesn’t support Secure Shell for repositories with Git LFS tracked files
notes.back: D) Azure Repos doesn’t support Secure Shell for repositories with Git LFS tracked files
notes.choicesExplained: A would break every repository, not only this one. B slows clones but doesn’t block a protocol. C isn’t a Git LFS requirement.
notes.explanation: This is a documented Git LFS limitation in Azure Repos.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work with large files in your Git repo”, “Git LFS limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Repos doesn't support Secure Shell (SSH) for repos with Git LFS tracked files.

notes.front: A push to GitHub is rejected because it adds a 150 MiB file that must stay versioned in the repository. What should you do?
notes.choices:
A) Upload it through the browser instead
B) Track the file with Git LFS
C) Split the push into two smaller pushes
D) Compress it into a zip archive
notes.back: B) Track the file with Git LFS
notes.choicesExplained: A the browser limit is lower still. C the file itself is over the limit, however it is pushed. D keeps a large binary in plain Git; archives are also the wrong fix.
notes.explanation: Files beyond GitHub’s limit must be tracked with Git LFS.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About large files on GitHub”, “File size limits”
notes.evidence: To track files beyond this limit, you must use {% data variables.large_files.product_name_long %} ({% data variables.large_files.product_name_short %}).

notes.front: A research group wants large data files kept out of Git’s objects and synced to its own server over rsync, with only stock Python and rsync installed. Which tool fits?
notes.choices:
A) git-sizer
B) Git LFS on Azure Repos
C) Scalar
D) git-fat
notes.back: D) git-fat
notes.choicesExplained: B stores content in the Git host’s LFS storage, not their rsync server. C tunes large repositories but doesn’t move files out. A only measures a repository.
notes.explanation: git-fat keeps fat files in its own store and syncs them to a remote set in `.gitfat` over rsync.
notes.source: Jed Brown, “git-fat README”, “Installation and configuration” (jedbrown/git-fat on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Set a remote store for the fat objects by editing `.gitfat`. [rsync] remote = your.remote-host.org:/share/fat-store

notes.front: An engineer joins a team with a huge repository but needs only two of its top-level folders. Which approach suits Scalar?
notes.choices:
A) `git clone`, then delete the other folders
B) `scalar diagnose`
C) `scalar clone --full-clone`
D) `scalar clone`, then widen the sparse-checkout to the two folders
notes.back: D) `scalar clone`, then widen the sparse-checkout to the two folders
notes.choicesExplained: A downloads everything first. C turns sparse-checkout off, so every file arrives. B gathers diagnostics; it doesn’t clone.
notes.explanation: `scalar clone` starts sparse with only top-level files, and you add the directories you need.
notes.source: Git project, “scalar documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A job writes thousands of generated files into one directory, and every small update makes the repository grow. What does the guidance recommend?
notes.choices:
A) Move all the files into Git LFS
B) Partition them into a nested layout such as year/month/day
C) Squash the commits that change them
D) Delete stale branches
notes.back: B) Partition them into a nested layout such as year/month/day
notes.choicesExplained: A moving many small files into Git LFS can make performance worse. C doesn’t change the tree object rewritten on each change. D addresses a different cause.
notes.explanation: A flat directory is one large tree object rewritten on every change; a nested layout keeps each directory small.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Oversized or flat directory structures” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you need to store a large amount of generated data in the repository, partition it into a nested layout such as _year/month/day_.

notes.front: A pipeline only builds the latest commit of a repository with years of history. Which clone option cuts its download most directly?
notes.choices:
A) A partial clone
B) A shallow clone
C) A full clone with `git-sizer`
D) `scalar register`
notes.back: B) A shallow clone
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps the full history. C measures size rather than reducing it. D starts maintenance on an existing clone.
notes.explanation: A shallow clone limits how much history is fetched, which the guidance says suits builds that need only the latest commits.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Speed up clones and fetches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A shallow clone limits how much history is fetched, which works well for CI that only needs the latest commits.

notes.front: An Azure Repos repository grew huge from old binaries. The team deleted branches and force pushed, but its size didn’t change. What is the only complete fix?
notes.choices:
A) Run `git gc` on every developer’s clone
B) Enable the Maximum file size policy
C) Recreate the repository and migrate just the content needed
D) Turn on Git LFS for the existing files
notes.back: C) Recreate the repository and migrate just the content needed
notes.choicesExplained: A doesn’t change server storage. B only stops new large files. D prevents future growth but leaves the old data on the server.
notes.explanation: Azure Repos storage is append-only, so previously committed data stays on the server.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Unused branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Force-pushing or deleting a branch doesn't reclaim that space. The only way to remove the data completely is to recreate the repository and migrate just the content you need.

notes.front: A job had one `checkout: self` step and scripts using the `s` folder. After a second `checkout` step is added, those scripts can’t find the files. Why?
notes.choices:
A) The second repository overwrote the first
B) With default paths, the first repository now sits in a subfolder of `s` named after it
C) Inline checkout syntax disables `self`
D) Multi-repo checkout needs a new agent
notes.back: B) With default paths, the first repository now sits in a subfolder of `s` named after it
notes.choicesExplained: A each repository gets its own folder. D isn’t a requirement. C `self` is still checked out.
notes.explanation: Adding a second checkout step changes the default path of the first repository.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Check out multiple repositories in your pipeline”, “Checkout path” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you are using default paths, adding a second repository checkout step changes the default path of the code for the first repository.

notes.front: An Azure Pipelines job must also check out a GitHub repository. How must it be declared?
notes.choices:
A) As a repository resource with `type: github` and a GitHub service connection as `endpoint`
B) Inline, as `- checkout: github://owner/repo`
C) With `checkout: none`
D) As a template reference with `@`
notes.back: A) As a repository resource with `type: github` and a GitHub service connection as `endpoint`
notes.choicesExplained: B inline syntax is only for Azure Repos Git in the same organisation. C checks out nothing. D uses templates, not source checkout.
notes.explanation: Repository types that need a service connection, such as GitHub, must be repository resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Check out multiple repositories in your pipeline”, “Repository resource definition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You must use a repository resource if your repository type requires a service connection or other extended resources field.

notes.front: Changes to a shared template repository keep breaking app pipelines. How do the app teams stay on a known version?
notes.choices:
A) Copy the scripts from the template repository
B) Leave `ref` unset so it follows `main`
C) Pin the repository resource’s `ref` to a tag, such as `refs/tags/v1.0`
D) Declare the template repository inline in a `checkout` step
notes.back: C) Pin the repository resource’s `ref` to a tag, such as `refs/tags/v1.0`
notes.choicesExplained: A scripts from the template repository can’t be used by the pipeline anyway. B follows `refs/heads/main`, the source of the changes. D doesn’t affect how templates are resolved.
notes.explanation: Pinning `ref` fixes the version of the template used.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use YAML templates in pipelines for reusable and secure processes”, “Store templates in other repositories” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you want to use a particular, fixed version of the template, be sure to pin to a `ref`. The `refs` are either branches (`refs/heads/<name>`) or tags (`refs/tags/<name>`).

notes.front: A user is in one group with Contribute set to Allow and another with Contribute set to Deny on the same repository. What is the result?
notes.choices:
A) Allowed, because Allow was set first
B) Allowed, because one group grants it
C) Not set, because the two cancel out
D) Denied, because Deny generally overrides Allow
notes.back: D) Denied, because Deny generally overrides Allow
notes.choicesExplained: A the order of assignment doesn’t matter. B ignores that Deny overrides Allow granted through another group. C Not set is a state you choose, not a result of conflict.
notes.explanation: A Deny for a group affects all its members, even when another group grants Allow.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Understand permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Deny** generally overrides **Allow**, including permissions inherited or granted through another group. When you deny a permission for a group, the denial affects all members of that group.

notes.front: A new security group needs the same permissions on every Git repository in a project, including future ones. Where do you set them?
notes.choices:
A) On each repository in turn
B) On each branch of each repository
C) At the All Repositories level
D) In a branch policy
notes.back: C) At the All Repositories level
notes.choicesExplained: A misses repositories created later and repeats the work. B sets branch permissions, not repository ones. D controls merging, not access.
notes.explanation: Permissions at All Repositories apply to every Git repository in the project, and individual repositories inherit them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Open repository security” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Set permissions at the All Repositories level to apply them to every Git repository in a project, or set permissions for an individual repository. Individual repositories inherit permissions from the project-level Git repositories entry.

notes.front: A user should bypass policies only when completing pull requests. Bypass policies when completing pull requests is Allow. What should Bypass policies when pushing be, if nothing else grants it?
notes.choices:
A) Allow
B) Not set
C) Deny, always
D) Inherited from Exempt from policy enforcement
notes.back: B) Not set
notes.choicesExplained: A would let the user push directly. C is only needed to override an applicable Allow. D the old permission no longer exists; it was replaced.
notes.explanation: The docs say to leave it Not set, and use Deny only to override an applicable Allow.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set Git repository permissions”, “Configure policy bypass permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To let a user bypass policies only when completing pull requests, set **Bypass policies when completing pull requests** to **Allow**. Leave **Bypass policies when pushing** as **Not set** if the user doesn't receive Allow through another assignment.

notes.front: A build engineer needs a lightweight tag on a commit in Azure Repos. Where can she create it?
notes.choices:
A) The Tags view in the web portal
B) The Commits view in the web portal
C) A call to the Azure DevOps annotated-tags service
D) The Git command line
notes.back: D) The Git command line
notes.choicesExplained: A and B create only annotated tags. C creates annotated tags.
notes.explanation: The web portal creates only annotated tags; the docs point to the Git command line for lightweight ones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Git tags”, “Create tag” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can only create annotated tags in the web portal or Visual Studio. To create a lightweight tag, you can use Git command line.

notes.front: You edited `README.md` but haven’t committed, and want it back as it was at the last commit. Which command fits?
notes.choices:
A) `git checkout README.md`
B) `git revert HEAD`
C) `git reset --soft HEAD~1`
D) `git reflog`
notes.back: A) `git checkout README.md`
notes.choicesExplained: B reverses the last commit rather than your uncommitted edits. C moves the branch back a commit and keeps changes. D only shows reference history.
notes.explanation: It reverts only that file, to its last committed version.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Discard uncommitted changes to a file” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use the Git checkout command to discard uncommitted changes to a file by reverting the file to its last committed version

notes.front: Your last three commits are local, unpushed and wrong; you want them gone and your files as they were before them. Which command fits?
notes.choices:
A) `git revert` each commit
B) `git reset --hard` to the commit before them
C) `git reset --soft` to the commit before them
D) `git checkout <file>` for each file
notes.back: B) `git reset --hard` to the commit before them
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps the commits and adds more. C keeps the changes staged. D doesn’t move the branch.
notes.explanation: Resetting is fine here because the commits were never shared, and `--hard` discards the later changes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Revert a branch to a prior state” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The --hard flag tells Git to reset the branch to the specified commit, and to discard all subsequent changes. Be careful with this option since you can lose work using it.

notes.front: A bad commit was pushed to the shared `main` an hour ago and colleagues have pulled it. How do you undo its changes?
notes.choices:
A) `git reset --hard` and force push
B) `git revert` the commit and push
C) Delete and restore the branch
D) `git checkout` the previous commit on `main`
notes.back: B) `git revert` the commit and push
notes.choicesExplained: A rewrites shared history, so local and remote would no longer match. C restores the same commits. D doesn’t change the branch for others.
notes.explanation: Revert adds a new commit without altering history, so everyone’s branches still match.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Undo the changes made by a shared commit” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This approach is suitable for undoing the changes made by a shared commit because Git revert won't alter the previous commit history, and so local and remote branch histories continue to match.

notes.front: After `git reset --hard`, a developer realises she needs a commit that was on her branch. What helps her find where the branch pointed before?
notes.choices:
A) Restore branch in the web portal
B) `git revert`
C) `git log --oneline`
D) `git reflog`
notes.back: D) `git reflog`
notes.choicesExplained: B needs a commit you can already name. C lists only commits still reachable from the branch. A is for deleted branches, not moved ones.
notes.explanation: The reflog records each update to the branch tip in the local repository, including the reset.
notes.source: Git project, “git-reflog documentation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: You restored a deleted release branch in Azure Repos, but pull requests into it now merge without review. Why?
notes.choices:
A) Restored branches are locked
B) The branch was restored at the wrong commit
C) Branch policies and permissions aren’t restored with the branch
D) Deleted branches lose their history after 30 days
notes.back: C) Branch policies and permissions aren’t restored with the branch
notes.choicesExplained: A locking isn’t part of a restore. B it is recreated at its last commit. D there’s no retention policy on deleted branches.
notes.explanation: Only the branch itself comes back, so its policies must be set again.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Restore a deleted Git branch from the web portal”, “Restore branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The branch gets recreated at the last commit to which it pointed. Branch policies and permissions do not get restored.

notes.front: You rebased a video out of your local history and now must overwrite the server copy. Which Azure Repos permission do you need?
notes.choices:
A) Contribute
B) Force push (preferred) or Admin
C) Edit policies
D) Create tag
notes.back: B) Force push (preferred) or Admin
notes.choicesExplained: A allows ordinary pushes but not server-level operations like rebasing history. D and C are unrelated.
notes.explanation: Rewriting server history needs more than normal push rights.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remove a large binary from your Git history to manage the size of cloned repositories”, “Rebase and force push” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To proceed, you need Force push (preferred) or Admin permissions on the repository.

notes.front: A file of customer phone numbers was committed a year ago and must be purged from every commit on GitHub. Which tool does GitHub’s procedure use?
notes.choices:
A) `git revert`
B) `git reset --hard`
C) `git filter-repo`
D) `git reflog expire`
notes.back: C) `git filter-repo`
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the file in history. B only moves one branch and can’t reach every ref. D prunes local reflog entries only.
notes.explanation: The purge rewrites every branch, tag and ref, which is what `git-filter-repo` is for.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Purging a file from your local repository's history using git-filter-repo”
notes.evidence: If you want to delete a specific file from all branches/tags/refs, run the following command

notes.front: Before purging a file from history, what does GitHub recommend doing with open pull requests?
notes.choices:
A) Leave them open; they update themselves
B) Merge or close them all first
C) Rebase them after the purge
D) Convert them to draft pull requests
notes.back: B) Merge or close them all first
notes.choicesExplained: A changed hashes give them different diffs, and comments may be lost. D and C don’t avoid the changed diffs.
notes.explanation: Changed commit hashes alter pull request diffs and can invalidate review comments.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “Side effects of rewriting history”
notes.evidence: Changed commit SHAs will result in a different PR diff, and comments on the old PR diff may become invalidated and lost, which may cause confusion for authors and reviewers. We recommend merging or closing all open pull requests before removing files from your repository.

notes.front: An access token was pushed to a GitHub repository. What should you do first?
notes.choices:
A) Revoke or rotate the token
B) Run `git-filter-repo` on the repository
C) Make the repository private
D) Delete the branch holding the commit
notes.back: A) Revoke or rotate the token
notes.choicesExplained: B rewrites history but the token still works until revoked. C and D leave the token valid and possibly still reachable.
notes.explanation: Once revoked or rotated the secret can’t be used, which may be enough without rewriting history.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing sensitive data from a repository”, “About removing sensitive data from a repository”
notes.evidence: if the sensitive data you need to remove is a secret (e.g. password/token/credential), as is often the case, then as a first step you need to revoke and/or rotate that secret. Once the secret is revoked or rotated, it can no longer be used for access, and that may be sufficient to solve your problem.

notes.front: When should you use `git revert` rather than `git reset` to undo a commit?
notes.back: When the commit was pushed and is in use by others: revert adds a reversing commit instead of rewriting history.
notes.explanation: Resetting suits returning a branch to a prior state before others rely on it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Undo changes”, “Undo changes” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Undo the changes made by a shared commit by creating a new commit that reverses the changes. Because this approach won't rewrite existing commit history, it's suitable for reversing changes made by commits that were pushed and are in use by others.

notes.front: How does a shallow clone differ from a partial clone in what it leaves out?
notes.back: A shallow clone leaves out older history; a partial clone keeps all history but leaves out file contents until needed.
notes.explanation: Either way the client downloads less, without changing the repository itself.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Optimize repository performance”, “Speed up clones and fetches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A shallow clone limits how much history is fetched, which works well for CI that only needs the latest commits. - A partial clone preserves the full history but downloads file contents only when needed.
